ideas.hypothesis: New public transport users whose first unfamiliar trip includes a negative experience (missed connection, wayfinding failure, crowding) will make fewer trips over the next six months than otherwise similar new users with a positive first trip, so the first-trip primacy effect predicts retention independently of service quality later on.

sources.role: mechanism: primacy effect of first impressions applied to unfamiliar public transport trips
measure: user-survey satisfaction items and the link between satisfaction and customer retention
finding: how a new system is made sense of and normalised (or not) in the first weeks of use

ideas.test: Recruit incoming university students (new to the city) at enrolment; within one week of their first public transport trip, survey them on that trip's experience (rated incidents, wayfinding ease, overall impression). Link consenting participants to smartcard tap records for 6 months and regress monthly trip counts on the first-trip score, controlling for home-campus accessibility, car access and later satisfaction measured at month 3.
ideas.disconfirming: First-trip experience scores show no association with trip counts at 3 and 6 months once later satisfaction and accessibility are controlled, or the association is as strong for later trips as for the first one (no primacy).

ideas.hypothesis: After fare abolition, fewer than one third of the additional public transport trips come from former car users; most come from walking, cycling and new trips, so fare-free schemes raise ridership far more than they cut car use.

sources.role: setting: Dunkirk network-wide fare-free scheme from September 2018 as a natural experiment
mechanism: cost shocks to car travel shift trips toward public transport, a contrast to fare-side price changes
setting: fare level changes as a price lever on public transport use

ideas.test: Intercept and household panel surveys in Dunkirk asking current riders how the same trip was made before fare abolition, combined with pre/post cordon car counts and comparison to a similar French agglomeration with fares unchanged (difference-in-differences on car counts and boardings).
ideas.disconfirming: Survey-based diversion shows that former car trips make up half or more of the new public transport trips, and car counts fall relative to the control city by a similar magnitude.

ideas.hypothesis: In an error correction model of monthly public transport demand anchored on labour force, the short-run response to fuel price increases is larger than the response to fuel price decreases, so ignoring this asymmetry explains why fuel prices appeared not to be cointegrated with demand.

sources.role: method: cointegration and error correction model of London public transport demand with labour force, population and oil price
finding: Melbourne patronage jumped during the 2005 fuel price surge
measure: national public transport performance statistics as a source of time series

ideas.test: Assemble 15+ years of monthly patronage for one metropolitan system (e.g. Melbourne or a Finnish city) with real retail petrol prices, employment and service-km. Estimate a symmetric ECM and an asymmetric ECM that splits price changes into positive and negative components; compare with Wald tests on asymmetry and out-of-sample forecast error.
ideas.disconfirming: Coefficients on positive and negative fuel price changes are statistically indistinguishable, and the asymmetric model does not improve out-of-sample forecasts.

ideas.hypothesis: A public transport accessibility index that weights stop service levels by the population density they serve will explain more variation in zone-level public transport mode share than a conventional unweighted index.

sources.role: method: spatial accessibility measure incorporating population density (note: retracted, so the method needs independent re-derivation)
finding: high population density and mixed uses cluster around accessible public transport in Zagreb
mechanism: urban form influences travel, with cautions about causal inference

ideas.test: For one metropolitan area, compute both indices at census-zone level from GTFS timetables and gridded population; regress census journey-to-work public transport share on each index (plus car ownership and income) and compare out-of-sample R-squared using spatial cross-validation.
ideas.disconfirming: The density-weighted index gives no gain, or a loss, in explained variance or predictive accuracy relative to the unweighted index.

ideas.hypothesis: Across cities of similar size and density, patronage per capita depends more on network structure (share of service-km on frequent, direct, connected routes) than on total service supply per capita.

sources.role: finding: comparator cities achieve higher trip rates than New Zealand cities without proportionately larger supply
mechanism: network planning for more effective public transport in New Zealand cities
method: comparison of network-plus-loop running modes and transfer designs

ideas.test: Build a dataset of 20-30 cities (including Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch and comparators) with GTFS-derived structure metrics (frequent-network share, route directness, transfer connectivity), service-km per capita, population density and annual boardings per capita; estimate a cross-sectional regression and check robustness with leave-one-out.
ideas.disconfirming: Service-km per capita dominates explanation of patronage and network structure metrics add no significant explanatory power once supply and density are included.

ideas.hypothesis: Opening a light rail line improves job accessibility and employment rates more in low-income neighbourhoods near new stops than in higher-income neighbourhoods near the same line.

sources.role: setting and finding: Tramlink in London and its association with social equity and spatial accessibility
method: spatial measurement of public transport accessibility
mechanism: infrastructure as a driver of economic outcomes

ideas.test: Difference-in-differences using small-area census data before and after line opening: small areas within 800 m of new stops versus matched areas elsewhere, interacted with baseline deprivation quintile; outcomes are employment rate and timetable-based jobs reachable in 45 minutes.
ideas.disconfirming: Gains in employment or job access are equal across income groups, or larger in higher-income areas near stops.

ideas.hypothesis: Reallocating street space to separated bicycle lanes on bus corridors increases bus passenger delay only where buses lose a dedicated lane or stop layout; where bus priority is kept, delay changes are negligible.

sources.role: method: quick assessment model of the impact of non-motorized lanes on public transport
setting: cycling promotion schemes as part of urban public transport systems
mechanism: conflicts between safety, accessibility and sustainability goals in shared street design

ideas.test: Use automatic vehicle location and passenger count data for bus corridors where bicycle lanes were added in one city, comparing before/after run times with untreated corridors, and split treated corridors by whether bus lanes and stop layouts were retained; convert run time change into passenger-hours of delay.
ideas.disconfirming: Corridors that kept bus priority still show significant increases in passenger delay comparable to those that lost bus lanes.

ideas.hypothesis: Residents who start using a new guided bus or bus rapid transit line increase daily walking and cycling minutes because of access and egress trips, compared with nearby residents who do not adopt it.

sources.role: setting: Cambridgeshire Guided Busway and how a new system becomes part of daily practice
method: exposure-response functions for health assessment of active travel
mechanism: planning of new communities to support health and wellbeing

ideas.test: Short cohort study: accelerometer and travel diary for one week before and six months after a new line opens, among adults living within 1 km and 1-3 km of stops; compare change in active travel minutes for adopters versus non-adopters, adjusting for baseline activity.
ideas.disconfirming: Adopters show no increase in total active travel, or the access walking is offset by reduced walking and cycling for other trips.

ideas.hypothesis: Stops and interchanges redesigned on public space principles (natural surveillance, lighting, active frontages, seating) will see lower perceived insecurity and fewer reported antisocial incidents than unchanged stops with similar patronage.

sources.role: mechanism: public space design strategies to improve passenger perception and reduce anti-social behaviour
measure: user survey of satisfaction with public transport attributes
setting: design of a new public transport terminal

ideas.test: Before/after comparison with matched controls: incident logs from operators and police for redesigned versus unchanged stations over two years, plus short intercept surveys of perceived safety at night at both groups.
ideas.disconfirming: Redesigned stops show no reduction in incidents or perceived insecurity relative to controls, or incidents move to nearby stops with no net change.

ideas.hypothesis: Franchised operation of rail and tram services raises government subsidies per passenger-km relative to public operation, after controlling for patronage growth and service changes.

sources.role: finding: Melbourne's privatised trams and trains cost more in public subsidies than continued public operation
method: benchmarking efficiency and effectiveness across comparator cities

ideas.test: Panel of Australian and New Zealand urban rail/tram systems over 20 years with annual subsidy, passenger-km and vehicle-km; estimate a fixed-effects model of subsidy per passenger-km with an indicator for franchised operation, plus a synthetic-control case for Melbourne.
ideas.disconfirming: Subsidy per passenger-km under franchising is equal to or lower than the counterfactual public-operation path once patronage and service levels are controlled.
